megalosaurus: Known only from fossils, Megalosaurus bucklandii lived during the Jurassic, roughly 168 to 166 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from limestone of the Taynton Limestone formation in the British Isles. It was a carnivore that weighed about 1000 kg as an adult, and it holds the distinction of being the first dinosaur ever given a scientific name.
common_raven: Found across the Palearctic, Nearctic, and Sahara, the common raven makes its home in mountains, tundra, forests, and deserts. Adults weigh about 1.2 kg, and their omnivorous diet lets them scavenge, hunt, and forage in nearly any setting. Ravens are known for their intelligence and their ability to mimic human speech, and they have long been linked with omens in folklore.
walia_ibex: The Walia ibex is a mountain-dwelling herbivore that weighs about 110 kilograms as an adult. It lives in herds across rugged highland terrain, feeding on plants and grasses. Though still alive today, the species is protected, and its long curved horns are a distinctive feature of the animal.
pangolin_sunda: Covered in overlapping keratin scales, the Sunda pangolin lives in jungles across Sundaland and Indochina. It is active at night and climbs trees with ease while hunting insects. An adult typically weighs about 5 kilograms. This species is still alive and is legally protected.
llama: Llamas (Lama glama) live in the Andes, moving across mountain slopes and grassland where they graze on herbs. An adult typically weighs about 140 kg. Living in herds, they have long been domesticated and used as pack animals, a role people have relied on since around 5000 BC, and their soft fur is valued too.
siberian_musk_deer: The Siberian musk deer is a small, shy animal of the taiga and mountain forests, ranging across Siberia, Japan, Korea, and the Mongolian steppe. It feeds on herbs and weighs about 13 kg as an adult. Males carry a pair of protruding fangs, and both sexes are hunted for the musk gland, which is prized for its scent.
colorado_river_toad: Active mostly at night, the Sonoran Desert toad lives across the deserts and badlands of western North America and Mexico. It is a meat eater, and an adult can reach about 0.25 kilograms. Its skin carries toxins, and it releases a secretion that can produce hallucinations, so predators and people are best advised to leave it alone.
sumatran_rhino: The Sumatran rhinoceros is a herbivore that lives in jungle and forest habitats across Indochina and Sundaland. Adults weigh about 700 kg, and this species still survives today. It is notable for its hairy coat and its horns, and it is a protected animal.
marmoset_common: Tree-dwelling and active during the day, the common marmoset lives in forest across its range in South America. It is an omnivore, eating a mixed diet, and a full-grown adult weighs about 0.35 kg. This species is not extinct and remains widespread in the wild.
russian_tortoise: Horsfield's Tortoise still roams the Kazakh steppe, Iran, Anatolia, and the Himalaya and Tibet. It lives in deserts, grasslands, and caves, and it feeds on plants. A full-grown adult weighs about 1.5 kg, and it digs burrows where it spends hot or dry periods in summer dormancy.
sloth_ground_jefferson: Jefferson's ground sloth roamed North America, with its range reaching as far north as Alaska and the Yukon. It lived in forests, where it fed on plants, and an adult could weigh about 1000 kg. Long claws marked it as one of the extinct megafauna, and it disappeared around 9000 BC.
hermanns_tortoise: Hermann's Tortoise lives across the Mediterranean and in parts of Europe, where it roams forests, grasslands, and coastal areas. It feeds on herbs and is active during the day. An adult typically weighs about 2 kg, and its domed shell protects it from predators. This species is still alive in the wild.
wrangel_mammoth: The Wrangel Island mammoth was a dwarfed population that survived on an icy tundra island far from the mainland. Adults weighed about 2800 kg and lived in herds, grazing on plants and using their long tusks and thick fur to endure the cold. These were among the last mammoths on Earth before the population died out around 1700 BC.
vegavis: A fossil relative of today's waterbirds, Vegavis iaai lived between 68 and 66 million years ago, during the Cretaceous. Its remains were pressed into mudstone of the Snow Hill Island formation in Antarctica. Adults weighed about 3 kg and fed on fish.
sloth_two_toed_southern: Slow and tree-bound, the southern two-toed sloth lives in the jungles of the Amazon and Orinoco basins. Adults weigh about 6 kg and feed on herbs while hanging from branches. Its coat often grows a green film of algae, and the species remains alive today.
nailtail_crescent: The Crescent nailtail wallaby once lived in the deserts of Australia, where it fed on herbs. Adults weighed about 3 kg. It was a nocturnal hopper, moving through the night in search of food. The species was declared extinct in 1956.
olenoides: Olenoides serratus lived during the Cambrian period, roughly 508 to 505 million years ago, and its fossils are preserved in shale of the Burgess Shale formation in northwestern North America. This extinct arthropod was a scavenger that reached an adult mass of about 0.08 kilograms. Its body was protected by a shell, and the fine detail of its scales has survived in the rock.
possum_common_brushtail: The common brushtail possum is found across Australia and Tasmania, where it makes its home in forest country. Its diet consists mainly of herbs, and an adult typically weighs about 3 kilograms. Living in the trees and active at night, it has a thick coat of fur and is still widespread today.
corn_snake: Found across eastern North America, the corn snake makes its home in the southern United States, including Florida and the Gulf region. It moves through forests, grasslands, and swamps, where it hunts small rodents by constriction. Adults typically weigh about 0.9 kilograms, and the species remains common in the wild today.
eastern_water_dragon: Active during the day, the Eastern Water Dragon makes its home across Australia, where it lives along rivers, through forests, and near the coast. Adults weigh about 1 kg, and they eat both plants and animals. This lizard climbs trees with ease and swims well, often escaping danger by diving into the water.
simosuchus: Simosuchus clarki lived in Madagascar during the Late Cretaceous, roughly 70 to 66 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Maevarano Formation. This short-snouted crocodyliform was a plant eater, and adults weighed about 10 kilograms, with a pug-like face that set it apart from its crocodile relatives.
green_iguana: Green iguanas range from southern Mexico through Central America and across the Amazon basin in the Neotropics. They favor jungle, forest, and river edges, where they climb trees and swim with ease. Active during the day, they feed on plants and can reach an adult mass of about 4 kg.
pademelon_tasmanian: Tasmanian pademelons are small, stocky wallabies found only on the island of Tasmania, where they make their homes in forest country. They feed mainly on herbs and grow to about 6 kilograms as adults. Active at night, they travel by hopping, and they remain a huntable species in the wild.
south_american_grey_fox: The South American grey fox, Lycalopex griseus, roams the Patagonian and Pampas regions as well as the Andes. It moves across grassland, desert, and mountain country, and it hunts mostly at night. Adults weigh around 4 kg, and this omnivore eats both plants and animals. Its thick fur helps it withstand the cold.
psittacosaurus: Psittacosaurus was a plant-eating dinosaur that lived between 125 and 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous period. Its fossils have been recovered from shale in the Yixian Formation of China's lowlands. An adult weighed about 20 kilograms, and it is recognized by its parrot-like beak and the bristles found on its tail.
blind_bear: Not a real species: Ursus speleus is the Pleistocene cave bear, which is extinct, and the facts given here conflict with that. The entry below follows your constraints but reflects the stated data, including that it is still alive and a fantasy variant. Blind Bear (Ursus speleus caecus) lives in Europe, where it roams caves and mountain terrain. It is an omnivore that weighs about 300 kg as an adult. Its thick fur helps it endure the cold, and it hibernates through the harsh months.
rabbit_amami: The Amami rabbit is a small, nocturnal herbivore that lives in forests within a narrow band of latitude and longitude on the Amami islands. Adults weigh about 2.5 kilograms, and they dig burrows where they rest during the day. Often called a primitive rabbit, it remains alive today and is legally protected.
didelphodon: Didelphodon vorax lived during the late Cretaceous, roughly 68 to 66 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone in the Hell Creek formation of the Great Plains. This carnivorous metatherian grew to about 5 kilograms as an adult and is noted for its strong bite.
hoary_fox: The hoary fox roams the savannas and grasslands of central South America, where it is still found today. Weighing about 3.5 kilograms as an adult, it is active at night and feeds mainly on insects, with termites forming a large part of its diet. Its grey-tipped fur gives the species its common name.
impala: Impalas roam the savannas of East and Southern Africa, and they also turn up in wooded areas nearby. These grazers feed on herbs and weigh about 55 kg as adults. They live in herds, and the males carry horns. Impalas remain common and are still alive today.
california_grizzly: The California grizzly once roamed forests, grasslands, and mountains across a wide stretch of the state. It was an omnivore, and adult males could weigh around 300 kilograms. Hunters pursued it for its fur, and the last confirmed individuals were shot between 1922 and 1924, with the subspecies declared extinct in 1924.
axolotl: Still found today, the axolotl is an amphibian that stays in water its whole life and keeps its juvenile features into adulthood. Its name is Ambystoma mexicanum, and it lives in the lakes and wetlands of a small region around Mexico City, where it is found nowhere else. Adults weigh about 0.2 kg and eat other small animals. It can regrow lost limbs, and it is legally protected.
sika: Sika deer live in Japan and Korea as well as the lowlands of China, where they make their homes in forested country. They feed on plants and grow to an adult weight of about 60 kg. Herds are common among them, and their antlers and status as a game animal have long made them valued by people, and they remain widespread today.
galapagos_tortoise_sierra_negra: The Sierra Negra giant tortoise makes its home on the Galapagos Islands, where it moves across both volcanic badlands and other island terrain. It feeds on plants and grasses, and a full-grown adult can weigh around 250 kilograms. Its high, domed shell helps set it apart, and this species is still living today.
shastasaurus: Shastasaurus pacificus lived during the Triassic, roughly 225 to 215 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from limestone of the Hosselkus formation in western North America. This carnivore grew to an adult mass of about 5000 kilograms. Lacking teeth, it is thought to have fed by suction.
freshwater_crocodile: Found across northern Australia, the freshwater crocodile makes its home in rivers, lakes, and wetlands. Adults typically weigh around 70 kilograms, and they are carnivores that hunt fish and insects. Their scales protect them as they swim through the water, and the species remains widespread today.
ross_seal: The Ross seal lives in the icy, cold waters around Antarctica, where it spends much of its life on pack ice. As a carnivore, it hunts in the ocean, and an adult can reach about 180 kg. Thick blubber helps it stay warm in the frigid environment. It is still alive and is not extinct.
leopard: Leopards range across Africa, southwestern Asia, the Indian subcontinent, Indochina, and Sundaland, living in savanna, jungle, forest, mountain, and desert habitats. These carnivores are nocturnal and climb trees with ease. Adults weigh about 60 kg, and some individuals have dark melanistic coats that appear almost black.
afghan_fox: The Afghan fox, known scientifically as Vulpes cana afghana, roams mountain country across its range. It eats a mixed diet of plants and animals, and an adult weighs about 1.5 kilograms. Active mostly at night, it is still alive in the wild and has a thick coat of fur.
mudpuppy: Spotted in rivers and lakes across eastern North America, the Common Mudpuppy ranges through the Canadian Shield and onto the Great Plains. This nocturnal amphibian keeps its feathery external gills for life and feeds on other creatures. An adult typically weighs about 0.3 kilograms, and the species remains widespread today.
ichthyostega: Ichthyostega lived during the Devonian, roughly 365 to 362 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Britta Dal Formation in Iceland and Greenland. This early four-limbed creature is thought to have been a carnivore weighing about 20 kilograms as an adult. Its body could both swim and walk, and each of its limbs bore seven toes.
dice_snake: The dice snake, Natrix tessellata, lives across Europe, the Mediterranean, Iran, and Anatolia. It favors rivers and lakes, where it swims well and hunts fish. Adults weigh around 0.3 kg, and the species is still alive and widespread.
citipati: Citipati is known only from fossils, dating to between 75 and 71 million years ago in the Cretaceous. Its remains were recovered from sandstone of the Djadochta formation on the Mongolian steppe. Adults weighed about 75 kg, and the diet is thought to have been omnivorous. Specimens preserved while brooding on their nests offer a rare glimpse of their parenting behavior.
caracal: The caracal ranges across Africa, Arabia, Iran and Anatolia, and the Indian subcontinent, where it roams savanna, desert, badlands, and grassland. An adult typically weighs about 14 kilograms. It hunts mostly at night, relying on a carnivorous diet, and its dark ear tufts and ability to leap help set it apart. It is still alive and widespread.
pyrenean_chamois: The Pyrenean chamois roams the high mountains of its range, where rocky slopes and open grassland provide its home. It feeds on plants and grasses, and adults weigh about 35 kg. Living in herds, this animal has horns and is still alive today, and it is also a species that may be hunted.
compsognathus: Turkey-sized and carnivorous, this fossil taxon lived in the Jurassic period roughly 150 to 148 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone of the Solnhofen formation in Europe, and adults weighed about 3 kg. One specimen preserves a small lizard in its belly, offering a rare glimpse of what it ate.
gharial: Slender-snouted and built for rivers, the gharial lives in the waterways of the Indian subcontinent. Its long, narrow snout is well suited to catching fish, which make up its diet. Adults can reach about 160 kg, and the species survives today under legal protection.
green_turtle: Adults of this species can reach about 160 kg, and they move between tropical seas across the Indian Ocean, the Indo-Pacific coast, and the western Atlantic. They spend time in warm ocean waters, along coasts, and around reefs, where they graze on seagrass. Although still living in the wild, they are protected because they have long been hunted for their edible meat.
water_monitor: The Asian Water Monitor is a living lizard found across the Indian subcontinent, Indochina, Sundaland, and Wallacea and New Guinea. It favors rivers, swamps, coasts, and jungle, where it swims well and eats both prey and carrion. Adults can reach about 20 kg.
majorcan_midwife_toad: The Majorcan Midwife Toad lives on the island of Majorca, where it makes its home in mountains and caves. It feeds on insects and weighs only about 5 grams as an adult. Scientists knew this small amphibian only from fossils until its living populations were discovered in 1977.
black_wildebeest: Roaming the open plains and grasslands of Southern Africa, the black wildebeest grazes on herbs and moves in herds. An adult typically weighs about 150 kg and carries curved horns that both sexes wear. This species is still alive today and is huntable, which makes it a familiar sight on managed reserves and farms.
dunkleosteus_marsaisi: Dunkleosteus marsaisi lived during the Devonian, roughly 380 to 375 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from limestone of the Hamar Laghdad Formation on the northern coast of Africa. This fossil fish was a carnivore that reached an adult mass of about 400 kilograms. It was an arthrodire, a group of armored placoderms, and it swam through ancient seas.
spiny_tailed_monitor: Tucked into the rocky scree and sandy desert of Australia, this small lizard weighs about 0.3 kilograms as an adult. It spends its days in crevices among the badlands and dry plains, where it hunts insects. The species is still alive and holds its own in the harsh country it calls home.
mesolimulus: Mesolimulus walchi was a horseshoe crab that lived during the Jurassic, roughly 152 to 148 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the limestone of the Solnhofen formation in Europe. Adults reached about half a kilogram, and the animal is known for the trails of marks it left behind, sometimes called death trails.
boa_constrictor: Found from Mexico and Central America through the Amazon basin, the boa constrictor lives in jungles, forests, and savanna. It is a meat eater that hunts mostly at night, coiling around prey and squeezing until it can no longer breathe. Adults can reach about 25 kilograms, and the species is still widespread today.
plesiosaurus: A marine reptile known only from fossils, this creature swam Jurassic seas roughly 200 to 190 million years ago. Its remains have been pulled from limestone of the Blue Lias formation in the British Isles. It was a carnivore that reached an adult mass of about 450 kg. Its skeleton was among the discoveries made by Mary Anning at Lyme Regis.
mangrove_monitor: The Mangrove Monitor is a lizard found across Wallacea, New Guinea, Australia, and Polynesia, where it lives along coasts, through jungle, and in swamps. It is carnivorous and typically weighs about 3 kg as an adult. Still alive and widespread, it climbs trees and swims with ease.
pinyon_jay: Pinyon jays are small, blue-gray birds found across western North America and into Mexico. They move through forests and open plains in flocks, weighing about 0.1 kilograms as adults. Their diet is mostly plant material, and they are known for being clever and sociable birds that travel together in large groups.
pampas_cat: Found across the Pampas, Gran Chaco, Andes, and Patagonia, this small wild cat roams both grasslands and mountain country. It hunts meat at night and weighs about 3.5 kilograms as an adult. Its dense fur helps it withstand the varied climates of its range, and it remains alive and widespread today.
olive_sea_snake: The olive sea snake makes its home on coral reefs in warm ocean waters, with much of its range in the Great Barrier Reef and the Coral Triangle. It feeds mainly on fish and grows to an adult mass of about 1.5 kilograms. Covered in scales and armed with venom, this species swims through the water and remains alive today.
geosaurus: Geosaurus giganteus is a fossil species from the Jurassic period, living between about 152 and 148 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone of the Solnhofen formation in Europe. This carnivore is often called a sea crocodile and grew to an adult mass of around 200 kilograms.
saw_scaled_viper: The saw-scaled viper lives across the Indian subcontinent, Arabia, the Sahel, and parts of Iran and Anatolia. It makes its home in deserts, badlands, and savanna, where it hunts small prey. Adults weigh about 0.1 kilograms, and this venomous snake is still widespread today. Its rough, saw-edged scales rub together to make a warning hiss, and it can move sideways across loose sand.
short_eared_dog: The short-eared dog roams the Amazon basin, moving through both dense jungle and swampy ground. It is a carnivore, and adults weigh around 9 kg. Shy and solitary, it is rarely seen, and its thick fur helps it keep out the damp of the forest.
hare_mountain: The mountain hare, Lepus timidus, ranges across Scandinavia, the Siberian taiga, the Alps, the British Isles, and northern Asia. It lives in tundra, taiga, and mountain country, and it feeds on herbs. Adults weigh about 3 kg, and the species is still alive today. In winter its coat turns white, and it is a huntable animal.
dolphin_humpback_pacific: Found along Indo-Pacific coasts, in the China lowlands, and across Sundaland, this toothed dolphin moves between coastal waters and rivers. It is a carnivore, and adults can weigh around 200 kg. Pods are typical of the species, and older individuals often take on a pinkish coloration. It remains alive today.
sumatran_tiger: The Sumatran Tiger roams jungles, forests, and swamps across the island of Sumatra. It is a carnivore that hunts other animals and can weigh up to about 120 kilograms as an adult. This tiger is still alive, is known for its dense fur, is a strong swimmer, and receives legal protection.
spotted_nutcracker: Hiding food for later is the spotted nutcracker's way of life. This bird ranges across Europe, the Siberian taiga, Scandinavia, and parts of Japan and Korea, moving between taiga and mountain forests. It feeds mainly on seeds and other plant matter, and it weighs about 0.18 kilograms as an adult. Clever and quick to learn, it is still going strong across its range.
bearded_seal: Bearded seals roam the icy waters of the Arctic Ocean and the North Pacific, where they feed on other creatures of the cold sea. An adult can weigh around 270 kilograms, and its thick layer of blubber helps it stay warm. Its long, whiskered snout is a distinctive feature, and it remains very much alive today.
beaded_lizard: The Mexican Beaded Lizard lives in Mexico and parts of Central America, moving through forests, deserts, and savannas. It is a meat eater that weighs about 1.2 kilograms as an adult. Its bead-like scales cover its body, it is venomous, it digs burrows, and it raids the eggs of other animals.
arabian_wolf: Roaming the deserts and badlands of Arabia, the Arabian wolf is a smaller subspecies of the gray wolf. Adults weigh about 20 kg and feed on meat. These wolves live in packs, have thick fur suited to harsh climates, and hunt mostly at night.
stone_marten: The stone marten makes its home across Europe, Iran, Anatolia, the Himalaya, Tibet, and the Mediterranean region. It lives in forests, mountains, and badlands, and it is active at night. Adults weigh about 1.7 kg, and this omnivore eats a varied diet while keeping its dense fur well insulated against cold climates.
alpine_chamois: The alpine chamois roams the mountains of the Alps, where it grazes on herbs across rocky slopes and high meadows. An adult typically weighs about 40 kilograms. It lives in herds, and both sexes carry short, hooked horns. The species remains widespread today and is huntable in many areas.
african_rock_python: The African rock python ranges across sub-Saharan Africa, from the Sahel to the savannas of East Africa. It makes its home in savanna, swamp, and forest, and it is a carnivore. Adults can reach about 55 kg, and this constrictor is at home in the water as well as on land.
rhamphorhynchus: Rhamphorhynchus is known only from fossils, which lived during the Jurassic period roughly 150 to 148 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone of the Solnhofen formation in Europe. This flying reptile fed on fish and weighed about half a kilogram as an adult. A long tail ending in a diamond-shaped vane set it apart from many of its relatives.
tenontosaurus: Tenontosaurus tilletti was a plant-eating dinosaur that roamed western North America between 115 and 108 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone in the Cloverly Formation. An adult could weigh around 1000 kilograms, and it was a favored meal for the small predator Deinonychus.
flatback_turtle: The flatback sea turtle lives in warm coastal waters, reefs, and ocean shelves, mainly around Australia, the Great Barrier Reef, and the Coral Triangle. Adults can reach about 80 kg, and they feed on meat, swimming with a broad, flattened shell. Unlike many of its relatives, this species stays within the Australian continental shelf, and it is protected, but it is still alive today.
japanese_sea_lion: The Japanese Sea Lion once lived along the coasts of Japan and Korea, where it hunted fish and other prey in cold ocean waters. Adults could weigh about 400 kg, and they moved together in herds, relying on a thick layer of blubber to stay warm. Sightings became rare in the 1950s, and the species was declared extinct in 1974.
corroboree_frog: Small and alpine, this amphibian lives in mountain country between roughly 35.5 and 36.5 degrees south and 148 to 149 degrees east. It feeds on insects and weighs only about 5 grams as an adult. Its skin is toxic, and the species is still alive today.
ground_squirrel_arctic: Found across Beringia, Alaska, the Yukon, and the Arctic, this squirrel makes its home in tundra landscapes. It eats both plants and animals, and an adult weighs about 0.75 kg. It digs burrows and hibernates through the long, cold months, and it remains widespread today.
mule_deer: Mule deer roam western and northwestern North America, reaching into Mexico and across the Great Plains. They make their homes in forests, badlands, and mountain country, feeding on herbs. A typical adult weighs about 80 kg, and the males grow antlers that make them a prized target for hunters.
asp_viper: The asp viper lives in the Alps, across Atlantic Europe, and around the Mediterranean. It favors mountain slopes and forest edges, where it hunts small prey. An adult typically weighs about 0.2 kilograms, and its body is covered in scales and armed with venom. It is still alive and widespread.
glass_frog: Perched on leaves above Central American streams, this small amphibian feeds on insects in jungle and river settings. Adults weigh only about two grams, and their see-through bellies let observers glimpse the organs inside. Still thriving in the wild, it spends its life in the trees.
giraffe_southern: Roaming the open savannas of Southern Africa, the southern giraffe is still thriving across its range. Adults can weigh around 1100 kilograms, and they browse on herbs and other plants. Living in herds, these tall animals are a familiar sight to hunters and travelers alike.
pyrenean_ibex: The Pyrenean ibex lived in the mountains of the Pyrenees, where it grazed on herbs across rocky slopes. Adults could weigh around 65 kg, and they moved in herds carrying impressive horns. Hunting pressure contributed to its decline, and the last known individual, called the bucardo, died in 2000.
eurasian_jay: The Eurasian jay lives across Europe and parts of the Palearctic and Indomalaya regions, where it favors wooded areas. It eats a mix of plant and animal foods and weighs about 0.17 kg as an adult. Known for burying acorns and for copying the calls of other birds, it is a clever forest dweller that is still widespread today.
dolphin_ganges: The Ganges river dolphin hunts in the rivers of the Indian subcontinent, where it feeds on fish and other small prey. Adults can weigh around 90 kilograms. Though it is nearly blind, it is still alive today and is a protected species. It is a freshwater toothed whale that navigates murky waters with sonar.
isotelus_maximus: Isotelus maximus was a trilobite, a fossil arthropod that lived in the seas of the Ordovician period between 455 and 450 million years ago. Its remains turn up in limestone of the Trenton Group in eastern North America, where it is known from many well-preserved shells. Adults reached about 2 kilograms, and it fed as a scavenger. Today it is the state fossil of Ohio.
zhenyuanlong: Zhenyuanlong lived roughly 125 to 122 million years ago during the Cretaceous. Its fossils were preserved in shale of the Yixian Formation in the lowlands of China. This carnivore weighed about 20 kg as an adult, and it was a short-armed winged dromaeosaur.
indian_narrow_headed_softshell: The Narrow-headed Softshell Turtle calls rivers of the Indian subcontinent home. It hunts by ambush, often burying itself in sand with only its eyes and snout showing. Its flat, soft-edged shell helps it glide through the water, and adults can reach a mass of about 100 kg.
pterodaustro: Pterodaustro guinazui was a pterosaur that lived between 112 and 100 million years ago during the Cretaceous. Its fossils have been recovered from limestone of the Lagarcito Formation in Patagonia and the Pampas. Adults weighed about 5 kilograms, and this flying reptile fed by filtering, using a dense row of comb-like teeth.
roe_deer: Roe deer roam across Europe, the British Isles, and parts of Iran and Anatolia, where they favor forested landscapes. These herbivores feed on a range of plants and typically weigh around 25 kilograms as adults. Though still thriving across their range, they are a huntable species, and males grow antlers that they shed each year.
eurasian_otter: The Eurasian otter ranges across Europe, the British Isles, Iran, Anatolia, the Indian subcontinent, and Indochina. It lives along rivers, lakes, wetlands, and coasts, where it hunts fish and swims with ease. Adults weigh about 10 kg, and this species is still alive, though it is protected and was once hunted for its dense fur. It is mostly active at night.
reeves_muntjac: Reeves's muntjac is a small deer that lives in the lowlands of China, where it makes its home in forest cover. It feeds on herbs and weighs about 15 kilograms as an adult. This species is still alive and can be hunted, and the males grow antlers.
marmot_alpine: Active during daylight hours, the Alpine marmot grazes on herbs across mountain grasslands in the Alps. Adults weigh about 4.5 kg and live in burrows, where they spend the long winter in hibernation. This species is still alive and remains common in its range.
javan_leopard: The Javan leopard roams jungle, forest, mountain, and island terrain across a range spanning roughly latitude -8.8 to -6 and longitude 105 to 114.7. Adults weigh about 50 kg, and they hunt meat as their main food. These cats are active at night, and dark melanistic coats are common among them. The species is still alive today.
hare_european: The European brown hare roams across Europe, Iran, and Anatolia, where it makes its home in open grassland. Adults weigh about 4 kg and feed on herbs. Still thriving, this solitary species is a swift runner that is also hunted by people.
hylonomus: Hylonomus lived during the Carboniferous period, roughly 312 to 310 million years ago, and it is the oldest known reptile. Its fossils turn up in mudstone of the Joggins Formation in eastern North America, often inside fossilized tree stumps. This small creature weighed about 0.02 kg as an adult and fed on insects. It is also linked to burrowing behavior.
common_reedbuck: Found across southern Africa and the East African savanna, the southern reedbuck lives in wetlands and grassland where it feeds on herbs. Adults typically weigh around 70 kilograms, and the species is still living in the wild. Males carry horns, and the animal is one that hunters are permitted to pursue.
eusthenopteron: Eusthenopteron was a lobe-finned fish that lived during the Devonian period, roughly 378 to 375 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the Escuminac Formation at Miguasha in eastern North America, preserved in sandstone. This carnivore grew to about 10 kilograms as an adult and swam through its waters. It is a close relative of the tetrapods, the group that later gave rise to four-limbed land animals.
tamaraw: The tamaraw is a small wild buffalo, Bubalus mindorensis, that lives on the island of Mindoro in the Philippines. It moves through both forest and grassland and feeds entirely on plants. Adults weigh about 300 kg, and the species is still alive today, though it is legally protected.
tomato_frog: The Tomato Frog is a round, bright red amphibian found in Madagascar, where it lives in forests and wetlands. It feeds on insects and can weigh around 0.2 kg as an adult. When threatened, it releases a sticky, toxic mucus from its skin, and it often retreats into a burrow to stay safe.
olive_ridley: Olive Ridley sea turtles roam tropical seas across the Indian Ocean and along the Indo-Pacific coast. Adults weigh about 40 kilograms, and they eat both plants and animals. Huge groups of females come ashore together to nest in a mass event called an arribada, and the species is protected so it can keep recovering.
dolphin_hector: Hector's dolphin is a small, toothed dolphin that lives close to the coast of New Zealand. Adults weigh about 45 kg, making it one of the smallest dolphins in the world. It hunts fish and other small prey and often travels in pods. Though still alive, it is a protected species.
flying_snake: The Paradise Tree Snake makes its home in the jungles of Sundaland and Indochina, where it spends most of its life in the canopy. It hunts small animals and is mildly venomous, though its bite poses little danger to people. Adults weigh about 0.15 kilograms, and the species flattens its body to glide from branch to branch.
vole_water: Found along rivers and wetlands across Europe, the British Isles, and the Siberian taiga, the European water vole is a plant-eater that weighs about 0.2 kg as an adult. It swims well and digs burrows in the banks of its watery home. This species is still alive today.
mauritian_giant_skink: Once found across the forests and coastlines of the Mascarene islands, this skink ate a varied diet of plants and small animals. An adult weighed around 0.1 kg. Introduced rats and cats are thought to have contributed to its disappearance, and the species was declared extinct in 1850 AD.
guadalupe_fur_seal: The Guadalupe fur seal lives along the coast and on islands within the area bounded by latitudes 22 and 35 north and longitudes 125 and 112 west. It is a carnivore, and adults reach about 100 kilograms. This species still survives today, gathers in herds, and is protected.
waterbuck: Roaming the savannas and wetlands of Africa south of the Sahara, the common waterbuck is a large herbivore that feeds on plants and grasses. An adult can weigh around 230 kilograms, and it lives in herds. Males carry long, curved horns, and the species is known to swim well, which is one reason it stays close to water.
bush_viper: Tree-dwelling and venomous, the hairy bush viper lives in the jungles of the Congo basin, where it hunts other animals. An adult weighs about 0.2 kilograms. Its rough, keeled scales give it a shaggy look, and it remains common in its native range.
dama_gazelle: The dama gazelle roams the Sahara and Sahel, living in open desert country where it grazes on herbs. An adult typically weighs about 65 kg. Though still alive, it is a protected species, and it lives in herds and carries horns.
massospondylus: Massospondylus was a prosauropod dinosaur that lived during the Jurassic, roughly 200 to 183 million years ago. Its fossils have turned up in sandstone of the Elliot Formation in Southern Africa. Adults weighed about 250 kg, and the animal fed on plants, with evidence of nesting activity found at Golden Gate.
galapagos_tortoise_santiago: The Santiago Giant Tortoise is a living species that calls the Galapagos home. Its high, domed shell helps it move through the island's rugged badlands, where it grazes on plants. An adult can weigh around 230 kilograms, making it one of the heavier residents of the archipelago.
kemps_ridley: At around 40 kilograms as adults, the Kemp's Ridley is the smallest sea turtle in the world. It lives in warm coastal waters of the Gulf of Mexico, the western Atlantic tropics, and the northern Atlantic, and it feeds on meat. Its populations are protected, and it is still alive today.
japanese_wolf: The Japanese wolf once roamed forests and mountains across the islands of Japan, where it lived in packs and hunted as a meat eater. Adults weighed about 15 kg, and their thick, small-bodied frames were built for rugged terrain. The last known specimen was recorded in 1905, and the subspecies is now considered extinct.
grey_rhebok: The grey rhebok is a slender antelope found in the mountains and grasslands of southern Africa. Weighing about 25 kilograms as an adult, it feeds on herbs and remains widespread today. Its straight, slim horns make it a species that hunters are permitted to pursue.
bush_hyrax: Bush hyraxes live in groups and are active during the day. They are found across the East African savanna, Southern Africa, and the Sahel, where they favor mountains and badlands. Adults weigh about 3 kilograms, and they feed on herbs. They remain widespread and are not extinct.
porcupine_north_american: The North American porcupine lives across much of North America in forests and taiga. An adult weighs about 8 kilograms, and it feeds on plants and herbs. It is nocturnal and spends much of its time in trees, protected by its quills. Its population remains healthy today.
banded_mongoose: Found across Africa south of the Sahara, the banded mongoose makes its home in savanna and grassland. Adults weigh about 1.5 kg, and they feed mainly on insects. These animals are active during the day, travel together in herds, and rest in burrows, and they remain widespread with no threat of extinction.
markhor: The markhor is a wild goat of mountains and rugged badlands, where it feeds on plants. Adult males weigh around 70 kg and carry long, twisted spiral horns. These animals live in herds and remain alive today, though they are huntable in parts of their range.
mongolian_gazelle: The Mongolian gazelle roams the open plains and grasslands of the Mongolian steppe and the eastern steppe, where it grazes on herbs. Adults weigh about 30 kilograms. These animals travel in herds and migrate across the land, and both males and females carry horns. The species is still alive and can be legally hunted in some areas.
bat_vampire_common: The common vampire bat lives across the Neotropics, from Central America down to Mexico, roaming forests, jungles, and caves. It is nocturnal and flies through the dark to feed on blood, weighing only about 0.04 kg as an adult. Because it can carry diseases, it is also considered a disease vector.
antarctic_fur_seal: Colonies of Antarctic fur seals gather along the rocky coasts of the subantarctic islands and reach into Antarctica itself. Their dense fur and thick layer of blubber keep them warm in icy seas, where they hunt fish and other prey. Adults can weigh around 100 kg, and they travel together in large herds.
helianthaster: Helianthaster rhenanus is a fossil starfish-like echinoderm from the Devonian period, roughly 400 to 395 million years ago. Its remains are preserved in shale of the Hunsrück Slate in Europe. It is thought to have been a carnivore, and adults weighed around 0.3 kg. Its name refers to its sun-star shape.
smooth_snake: The Smooth Snake makes its home across Europe, the British Isles, and Scandinavia, where it moves through grassland and forest. This slim constrictor feeds on other animals and is known to eat lizards. An adult weighs about 0.1 kg, and the species is still alive today.
falkland_wolf: The Falkland Islands wolf, also called the warrah, was the only native land mammal of the Falklands. It lived on island coasts and grasslands, hunted meat, and weighed around 20 kg as an adult. Its fearless nature and thick fur were noted before the species disappeared in 1876.
sloth_cuban_megalocnus: Megalocnus rodens once roamed the forests of the Caribbean, where it fed on plants and grew to about 150 kilograms. Despite its name, this island sloth was a dwarfed relative of much larger ground sloths elsewhere in the Americas. It disappeared around 2500 BC, one of the many extinct megafauna of island ecosystems.
saltasaurus: Saltasaurus loricatus was a plant-eating fossil species that lived during the Cretaceous, roughly 74 to 70 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from sandstone of the Lecho Formation in the Andes. Adults reached about 7000 kg, and their skin was protected by bony osteoderms.
mekosuchus_inexpectatus: The New Caledonian terrestrial crocodile was a short-skulled, land-dwelling crocodile that lived in forests, wetlands, and other habitats across the island. It was a meat eater, and adults weighed around 35 kilograms. Its scaly body and unusual terrestrial lifestyle set it apart from its relatives, but it vanished around the year 1000 AD, soon after humans arrived on the island.
chuckwalla: The common chuckwalla is a large, plant-eating lizard found in western North America and Mexico. It lives in deserts, badlands, and mountain country, where it is active during the daytime. When threatened, it wedges itself into rock crevices so firmly that it is hard to pull out, and it weighs about 1.5 kilograms as an adult.
rat_giant_gambian: Active only at night, the Gambian pouched rat digs burrows in forest and savanna across West Africa, the Sahel, and the Congo basin. It eats both plant and animal food and can grow to about 1.4 kilograms as an adult. Still widespread today, this species is also hunted by people in parts of its range.
sinraptor: Known only from fossils, Sinraptor dongi lived during the Jurassic, roughly 161 to 156 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from mudstone of the Shishugou Formation, a rock unit found in the Himalaya and Tibet regions. This Chinese allosauroid was a carnivore that reached an estimated adult mass of about 900 kilograms.
dolphin_risso: Found in oceans across the world, this toothed whale prefers deep water, from warm tropical seas to cold northern and southern waters. Adults can weigh around 400 kilograms. Living in pods, these dolphins hunt squid, and many individuals carry pale scars across their bodies.
peacock_softshell: The Peacock Softshell Turtle lives in rivers and swamps across Sundaland and Indochina. It eats both plants and animals, and adults can reach about 35 kg. Its shell is soft and leathery rather than hard, and it spends much of its time swimming. The species is still alive, though people in parts of its range value it as food.
leatherback_turtle: Leatherback turtles roam tropical seas across the North Atlantic, North Pacific, Indian Ocean, and South Pacific. Adults can reach about 450 kilograms, and they are carnivores that feed mainly on jellyfish. Their leathery shell sets them apart, and the species is protected, though it is still alive today.
sambar: Large deer of the Rusa genus, the sambar ranges across the Indian subcontinent, Indochina, Sundaland, and the China lowlands. It lives in forest and jungle, grazing on herbs, and an adult can weigh around 230 kg. Males grow impressive antlers, and the species is still widespread and hunted in parts of its range.
aardwolf: Found across the savannas and grasslands of East and Southern Africa, this nocturnal creature weighs about 10 kilograms as an adult. It digs burrows for shelter during the day and feeds mainly on insects, especially termites, which it laps up with a sticky tongue. Its shaggy fur and long mane give it a distinctive look, and it remains very much alive today.
sand_rat_fat: The fat sand rat makes its home in deserts, ranging across the Sahara, the North African coast, and the Nile valley. It is a herbivore that feeds on plants and is active during the day. An adult weighs about 0.17 kg, and the species lives in burrows and is still alive today.
taruca: The taruca roams the high Andes, where it grazes on herbs across mountain slopes. Adults weigh about 65 kilograms, and males carry antlers that make them a recognizable sight on the rocky heights. Though still living in the wild, this deer is a species that hunters may pursue.
himalayan_pit_viper: The Himalayan pit viper lives across the Himalaya and Tibet, where it hunts in mountain country. It feeds on other animals and typically weighs around 0.3 kilograms as an adult. This venomous snake is known for its ability to live at high altitudes, and it remains widespread today.
seychelles_giant_tortoise_sumeirei: The Seychelles saddle-backed tortoise once roamed island forests in the Seychelles, where it grazed on plants and grew to roughly 110 kg as an adult. Overharvesting by people removed it from its island home, and the species was declared extinct around 1900. Its high-domed, saddle-shaped shell is a reminder of how quickly a large animal can disappear when hunting goes unchecked.
rhinoceros_hornbill: The rhinoceros hornbill makes its home in the jungles of Sundaland, where it spends most of its life in the trees. Adults weigh about 2.5 kg, and they feed mainly on fruit. The species is still alive, and its large casque on the upper bill sets it apart from other hornbills.
chipmunk_eastern: The eastern chipmunk makes its home across the forests of eastern North America, where it digs a burrow and stays active during the day. This small rodent weighs about 0.1 kilogram as an adult and eats a varied diet of both plants and animal matter. It remains widespread and common in the wild today.
adelophthalmus: Adelophthalmus lived during the Carboniferous period, roughly 307 to 306 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from shale of the Francis Creek formation at Mazon Creek in eastern North America. This carnivore reached about 1 kg as an adult and was a swimmer that tolerated brackish water.
diplocaulus: Diplocaulus lived during the Permian, roughly 290 to 272 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. This carnivore grew to about 5 kg as an adult. It swam through its watery habitat, and its most striking feature was a boomerang-shaped head.
eogyrinus: Eogyrinus was a crocodile-like embolomere that lived during the Carboniferous, roughly 315 to 305 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Coal Measures in the British Isles. Reaching about 4.5 metres in length and weighing around 90 kilograms, this carnivore was a strong swimmer.
otodus_angustidens: Known only from fossil teeth and a few vertebrae, this mega-toothed shark lived in the seas of the Eocene and Oligocene, roughly 34 to 23 million years ago. Its remains have turned up in marine sediments of the Chandler Bridge Formation in eastern North America. Estimated at around 2000 kg as an adult, it was a carnivore that swam through these ancient waters.
icaronycteris: Known from fossils preserved in shale of the Green River Formation in western North America, this creature lived roughly 52 to 50 million years ago during the Eocene. It weighed about 0.03 kilograms as an adult and fed on insects. Flying through the night, it is considered an early echolocating bat.
edestus: Edestus heinrichi was a fossil fish that lived during the Carboniferous period, roughly 310 to 305 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone of the Carbondale Formation in eastern North America. This meat-eating swimmer grew to about 2 to 3 meters long and weighed around 200 kilograms, and it carried scissor-like tooth whorls.
megalonyx: Megalonyx jeffersonii was a fossil ground sloth that lived during the Pliocene, roughly 5 to 0.013 million years ago. Its remains have turned up in the tar deposits of the Rancho La Brea formation in western North America. Adults weighed about 1000 kilograms, and the animal fed on plants while its long claws helped it manage life in forested country.
barylambda: Barylambda lived during the Paleocene, roughly 58 to 56 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Fort Union Formation in western North America. This herbivore was a heavy pantodont that could reach an adult mass of about 650 kilograms. Its bulk marks it as one of the larger animals of its time.
dorudon: Dorudon atrox was a fossil whale that lived during the Eocene, roughly 37 to 34 million years ago. Its remains come from the Birket Qarun Formation at Wadi Al-Hitan in the Nile valley, where they were preserved in mudstone. This carnivorous archaeocete reached about 5 meters in length and weighed around 1500 kilograms as an adult, and it was a capable swimmer.
aetiocetus: Aetiocetus lived in the Oligocene, roughly 28 to 25 million years ago, and its fossils have been pulled from marine sediments of the Alsea Formation in the Pacific Northwest. This toothed relative of modern baleen whales swam through ancient seas and fed on other animals. An adult could reach about 1500 kilograms.
orthacanthus: Orthacanthus texensis was a freshwater shark that lived during the Permian, between roughly 290 and 272 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. Adults reached about 60 kilograms, and the animal hunted meat while swimming through its waters with a long, eel-like body and a spine on its head.
oreopithecus: Oreopithecus lived in what is now Europe during the Miocene, roughly 8 to 7 million years ago. Its fossils were found in coal deposits of the Baccinello-Cinigiano Basin, in the Ribolla area. Adults weighed about 30 kg, and this tree-dwelling ape is thought to have eaten fruit while living on an island.
eremotherium: Eremotherium laurillardi was a giant ground sloth that roamed during the Pleistocene, between 2.5 and 0.013 million years ago. Its fossils have turned up in mudstone at Santa Fe River sites in Florida and along the Gulf region. Plant-eating and weighing about 3000 kg as adults, it carried large claws that marked it as a true heavyweight of its time.
pezosiren: Pezosiren was a fossil sea cow that lived during the Eocene, roughly 50 to 47 million years ago. Its remains come from sandstone of the Chapelton Formation in the Caribbean. It was a plant eater weighing about 200 kilograms as an adult, and it could both swim and walk on its four legs.
eryops: Eryops was a large amphibian that lived during the Permian period, roughly 295 to 272 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. Adults could reach about 2 meters in length and weighed around 90 kilograms, and they are thought to have hunted meat while moving both on land and through water.
maiacetus: A fossil whale from the Eocene, living roughly 47 to 46 million years ago, Maiacetus was found preserved in limestone of the Habib Rahi Formation on the Indian subcontinent. This carnivore weighed around 600 kilograms as an adult and could both swim and walk. A pregnant specimen reveals that it gave birth head-first on land.
rhizodus: A giant lobe-finned fish from the Carboniferous, Rhizodus lived roughly 340 to 330 million years ago. Its fossils have turned up in the East Kirkton Limestone of the British Isles. Reaching about 7 metres long and weighing around 300 kilograms, it was a meat-eater that swam through freshwater habitats.
helladotherium: Helladotherium was a short-necked giraffid that lived in Europe during the Miocene, roughly 9 to 7 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Pikermi Formation. Adults weighed around 800 kg, and the animal is thought to have grazed on plants while living in herds.
bullockornis: Bullockornis planei was a flightless bird that lived in what is now Australia during the Miocene, roughly 12 to 10 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from limestone of the Camfield Beds formation. Adults reached about 250 kg, and the animal was omnivorous, earning it the nickname "demon duck of doom."
prionosuchus: Prionosuchus was a fossil amphibian from the Permian period, living roughly 280 to 270 million years ago. Its remains come from sandstone of the Pedra de Fogo Formation in South America. It fed on fish and is thought to have reached a mass of about 800 kg, swimming through its waters with a long, gharial-like snout.
hyracodon: Hyracodon nebraskensis was a herbivore that roamed the Great Plains during the Eocene, between roughly 34 and 30 million years ago. Its fossils turn up in mudstone of the White River Group, in the Chadron and Brule Formations. Adults weighed about 150 kilograms, and the animal earned its nickname as a running rhino for its fast, plains-dwelling way of life.
gastornis: A flightless bird that stood about 2 meters tall, Gastornis lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 56 to 50 million years ago. Its fossils have turned up in the mudstone of the Argiles de Meudon formation. Adults reached around 150 kilograms, and the animal likely fed on plants using its massive beak.
epicyon: Epicyon haydeni was a fossil carnivore from the Miocene, roughly 10 to 7 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from sandstone of the Ash Hollow Formation within the Ogallala Group on the Great Plains. Weighing about 150 kg as an adult, this bone-crushing dog was a formidable meat eater.
mene_rhombea: The Bolca moonfish lived during the Eocene, roughly 50 to 49 million years ago, and its remains are preserved in the limestone of the Bolca Formation, known locally as Pesciara, in Europe. This fossil fish had a deep body and swam through its waters, feeding on insects. Adults reached about 0.5 kg.
megistotherium: Megistotherium was an extinct carnivore that lived along the northern African coast during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 18 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from limestone of the Gebel Zelten Formation. Adults may have weighed around 880 kilograms, making it a huge hyaenodont and one of the largest meat-eaters of its time.
dominican_malaria_mosquito: Preserved in Dominican amber from the La Toca Formation of the Caribbean, this fossil mosquito lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 15 million years ago. Adults fed on nectar and weighed about 0.00001 kg. Specimens in the amber have also been found carrying fossil malaria parasites.
inostrancevia: Inostrancevia was a gorgonopsian, a group of carnivores that lived during the Permian. Adults reached about 3.5 meters in length and weighed roughly 300 kilograms, and its long saber teeth made it an apex predator of its time. Its fossils come from mudstone of the Salarevo Formation in Europe, dating to 254 to 252 million years ago.
dimetrodon_grandis: Dimetrodon grandis is a fossil species from the Permian period, roughly 280 to 272 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. Adults reached about 300 kilograms and measured up to 3.5 meters long, making it the largest sail-backed predator of its kind, and it was a carnivore.
diplocynodon: A small alligatoroid that lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 48 to 47 million years ago. Its remains have been found in shale of the Messel Pit Formation. It was a carnivore that swam, and adults weighed around 30 kg.
eritherium: Eritherium azzouzorum lived during the Paleocene, roughly 60 to 58 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the Ouled Abdoun Phosphate Basin on the northern coast of Africa, in marine sediment. This herbivore weighed about 5 kg as an adult and is the earliest known proboscidean.
theropithecus: The giant gelada was a heavy, ground-dwelling monkey that lived in herds across the East African savanna during the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 0.3 million years ago. Adults reached about 70 kilograms, and its remains have been recovered from sandstone in the Olduvai Gorge Bed I and Bed II formations. It fed mainly on herbs, and its fossils show it moved and foraged on the ground.
dominican_stingless_bee: Preserved in amber from the La Toca Formation of the Caribbean, this fossil bee lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 15 million years ago. It belongs to a group of stingless bees and fed on nectar. Adults weighed about 0.0001 kilograms, and their bodies were sealed in resin, which kept them intact for millions of years.
machairodus: Known only from fossils, this saber-toothed cat lived in Europe during the Miocene, roughly 9 to 7 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from mudstone of the Pikermi Formation. It was a carnivore, and adults weighed about 250 kilograms.
pachydyptes: Pachydyptes ponderosus was a giant penguin that lived during the Eocene, roughly 36 to 34 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the Kokoamu Greensand formation in New Zealand, where they were preserved in marine sediment. Adults reached about 80 kilograms, and this swimmer fed on fish.
llallawavis: Llallawavis scagliai lived in what is now Argentina around 3.5 to 3 million years ago, during the Pliocene. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Chapadmalal Formation in Patagonia and the Pampas. This flightless terror bird stood about 1.2 metres tall, weighed roughly 18 kilograms as an adult, and was a carnivore.
homotherium_latidens: Lived in the Pliocene, roughly 4 to 0.028 million years ago. Its fossils have turned up in the Cromer Forest-bed Formation of the British Isles, preserved in sandstone. A carnivore with an adult mass of about 220 kg, it had long saber-like teeth and was built for running, and it may have hunted in packs.
dinofelis: Dinofelis barlowi was an extinct cat from the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 1 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from limestone deposits of the Swartkrans Formation in Southern Africa. Despite its saber-like canines, this carnivore was a false saber-tooth, and adults may have reached about 130 kilograms.
lystrosaurus_maccaigi: Lystrosaurus maccaigi lived during the Permian, roughly 253 to 251 million years ago, and its fossils turn up in mudstone of the Teekloof Formation in Southern Africa. This plant eater weighed about 90 kilograms as an adult and had tusks. It is thought to have burrowed and lived in herds, and it thrived after the Great Dying, the mass extinction that wiped out most life on Earth.
brontotherium: Roaming the Great Plains during the Eocene, this fossil taxon lived between 38 and 34 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from mudstone in the White River Group, specifically the Chadron and Brule Formations. An adult weighed around 3000 kg and fed on herbs, and it is thought to have moved in herds. Its Y-shaped nasal horn earned it the nickname thunder beast.
aegyptopithecus: An extinct primate known from fossils, Aegyptopithecus lived in the Oligocene, roughly 30 to 29 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from sandstone of the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region of the Nile valley. Adults weighed about 6 kg, and the animal was a tree-dwelling early catarrhine that fed mainly on fruit.
eremopezus: Eremopezus eocaenus was a fossil animal from the Eocene, living roughly 37 to 34 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from sandstone of the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region, near the Nile valley. It was omnivorous, grew to about 200 kilograms, and stood around 3 meters tall without the ability to fly.
presbyornis: An extinct fossil bird from the Eocene, living roughly 53 to 48 million years ago, Presbyornis is known from shale of the Green River Formation in western North America. Adults weighed about 4 kg, and the species was able to both fly and swim. It was a flamingo-like relative of ducks that likely fed by filtering food from water, and it may have moved in herds.
stegotetrabelodon: Long before modern elephants, this herbivore roamed what is now the North African coast during the Miocene, roughly 7 to 5 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Sahabi Formation. An adult weighed about 4000 kilograms, and it carried four tusks, making it one of the earliest known members of the elephant family.
pulmonoscorpius: Pulmonoscorpius kirktonensis was a fossil scorpion-like arachnid that lived during the Carboniferous period, roughly 335 to 330 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from the East Kirkton Limestone formation in the British Isles, where the rock preserved them within layers of limestone. This carnivore grew to about 0.7 metres in length and weighed around 2 kilograms as an adult.
teleoceras: Teleoceras major lived during the Miocene, roughly 12 to 11 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the Ashfall Tuff at the Ashfall Fossil Beds in the Great Plains, where they were preserved in volcanic ash. Adults weighed about 1500 kg, and this herbivore is thought to have spent much of its time in wetlands, moving through water much like a hippo does.
icadyptes: Icadyptes salasi lived roughly 42 to 36 million years ago during the Eocene, and its remains have been recovered from marine sediments of the Otuma Formation in the Paracas region of the Andes. This fossil penguin fed on fish and was a strong swimmer, moving through the water with its long beak. Adults reached an estimated mass of about 45 kilograms.
mesosaurus_karoo: Mesosaurus was a small freshwater reptile that lived in the Permian period, roughly 280 to 275 million years ago. Its fossils come from shale of the Whitehill Formation in the Karoo Supergroup of Southern Africa. It fed on fish, and adults weighed about 1 kg. Its body was built for swimming, and its long, slender jaws and stretched body plan set it apart from many of its relatives.
diatryma: The massive bird known as Diatryma lived during the Eocene, roughly 56 to 53 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Willwood Formation in the Bighorn Basin of western North America. Standing about 2 meters tall and weighing around 175 kilograms, it could not fly, and it was an herbivore with a huge beak.
rubidgea: Rubidgea was a carnivorous fossil animal that lived in what is now Southern Africa during the Permian period, roughly 256 to 254 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from mudstone of the Teekloof Formation in the Karoo Supergroup. Weighing about 300 kilograms as an adult, it was the largest gorgonopsian known from the Karoo, and it carried long saber teeth.
phareodus: Phareodus testis lived in the freshwater lakes of western North America during the Eocene, roughly 53 to 48 million years ago. Its fossils are preserved in the shale of the Green River Formation. This carnivorous bonytongue was a swimmer that grew to an adult mass of about 5 kilograms.
stegodon_orientalis: Roaming the lowlands of China during the Pleistocene, this fossil elephant relative lived between 2 and 0.05 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone deposits in the Liucheng Gigantopithecus Cave formation. Adults weighed around 5000 kilograms, and the animals grazed on herbs, moved in herds, and were able to swim, as shown by their ridged teeth.
purussaurus: Purussaurus lived in what is now the Amazon basin between 13 and 8 million years ago, and its remains have been recovered from mudstone of the Solimões Formation. This extinct crocodilian was an apex predator that could swim and reached a length of about 11 meters. Adults weighed roughly 8400 kilograms, and it fed on meat.
darwinius: Darwinius masillae lived in the trees of Europe during the Eocene, between 48 and 47 million years ago. Its fossils were preserved in shale of the Messel Pit Formation, and adults weighed about 0.9 kg. Its diet is recorded as frugivorous, and it was a lemur-like adapiform that often nicknamed "Ida."
arctocyon: Arctocyon primaevus lived in Europe during the Paleocene, roughly 60 to 57 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Sables de Cernay formation. Adults weighed about 100 kg, and this omnivore had a bear-like build along with hooves.
gigantophis: Gigantophis was a giant snake that lived during the Eocene, roughly 40 to 37 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region of the Nile valley, preserved in sandstone. This 10-metre madtsoiid was a carnivorous constrictor that could reach an adult mass of about 1000 kilograms.
kumimanu: Kumimanu biceae was a giant penguin that lived in the seas of what is now New Zealand during the Paleocene, roughly 60 to 56 million years ago. Its fossils were found in marine sediments of the Waipara Greensand formation. Adults reached about 100 kilograms, and the bird fed on fish while swimming through the water.
genyornis: A flightless bird from the Pleistocene, Genyornis newtoni stood about 2 meters tall and weighed roughly 230 kilograms as an adult. Its fossils were preserved in mudstone sediments at Lake Callabonna in Australia. It is thought to have been a herbivore, and it belonged to the group of birds known as mihirungs.
daeodon: Daeodon shoshonensis was a giant entelodont that lived in the Great Plains during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 19 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Harrison Formation. Adults weighed about 750 kilograms, and the animal was omnivorous.
westlothiana: Westlothiana lizziae is a fossil species from the Carboniferous, roughly 335 to 330 million years ago. Its remains were preserved in limestone of the East Kirkton Limestone formation in the British Isles. This small creature weighed about 0.01 kilograms and fed on insects, and it is nicknamed Lizzie the Lizard.
aepycamelus: Aepycamelus giganteus was a giraffe-like camel that lived during the Miocene, roughly 12 to 6 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Ogallala Group, within the Ash Hollow Formation of the Great Plains. This herbivore grew to an adult mass of about 700 kilograms.
leptictidium: Leptictidium lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 48 to 47 million years ago, and its remains have been recovered from the shale of the Messel Pit Formation. This insect eater weighed about 1 kilogram as an adult. It is thought to have moved by hopping on its hind legs.
mioplosus: Mioplosus labracoides lived during the Eocene, roughly 53 to 48 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from shale of the Green River Formation in western North America. This perch-like fish swam through its waters as a carnivore, growing to about 1 kilogram as an adult.
ouranopithecus: Ouranopithecus is known only from fossils, and it lived in Europe during the Miocene, roughly 9.6 to 8.7 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from mudstone of the Ravin de la Pluie Formation. This ground-dwelling ape is thought to have eaten fruit and weighed around 90 kilograms as an adult.
barbourofelis: Barbourofelis fricki was a saber-toothed false-cat that lived during the Miocene, roughly 9 to 7 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Ogallala Group, specifically the Ash Hollow Formation, across the Great Plains. This carnivore was a meat eater that weighed about 130 kilograms as an adult.
sivapithecus: Sivapithecus indicus lived during the Miocene, roughly 12 to 8 million years ago, and its remains have been recovered from the Siwalik Group, including the Nagri and Dhok Pathan Formations of the Indian subcontinent. Fossils are preserved in sandstone from these deposits. Adults weighed about 40 kilograms, and this fruit-eating ape spent much of its time in trees, making it a relative of the orangutan.
odobenocetops: A tusked, walrus-like dolphin from the Pliocene, Odobenocetops peruvianus lived roughly 4 to 3 million years ago. Its fossils come from marine sediments of the Pisco Formation in the Andes. This carnivore reached an adult mass of about 1500 kilograms and was a swimmer.
jonkeria: Jonkeria truculenta was a large predatory dinocephalian that roamed what is now Southern Africa during the Permian period, roughly 265 to 260 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Abrahamskraal Formation within the Karoo Supergroup. Adults weighed about 1000 kilograms, and the animal was a meat eater.
protemnodon: Protemnodon anak was a robust kangaroo that lived during the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 0.04 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone in the Darling Downs deposits, known as the Chinchilla Sand formation, in Australia. Adults reached about 130 kilograms, and this herbivore fed on plants.
hibbertopterus: Hibbertopterus was a giant sea scorpion relative that lived during the Carboniferous, roughly 330 to 320 million years ago. Its fossils turn up in mudstone of the Coal Measures in the British Isles. Measuring about 1.8 metres long and weighing around 60 kilograms as an adult, it scavenged on the seafloor and left behind trackways that show it walked.
anancus: Anancus arvernensis roamed Europe during the Pliocene, between about 4 and 2 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone layers of the Upper Valdarno Basin, where the animal was preserved among the sediments. Adults weighed around 3500 kilograms and fed on plants, while their straight tusks grew to roughly 3 metres long.
amphicyon_ingens: Amphicyon ingens lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 18 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Harrison Formation on the Great Plains. This carnivore was a meat eater that reached an adult mass of about 550 kilograms. Often called a bear dog, it was the largest member of its family, the amphicyonids.
allodesmus: Allodesmus kernensis was a large marine mammal that lived in the Miocene, roughly 16 to 15 million years ago. Its fossils come from the Round Mountain Silt, part of the Sharktooth Hill Bonebed in western North America, where they were buried in marine sediment. Adults weighed about 1000 kilograms, and this carnivore swam the coast as a relative of the giant sea lion.
nimbadon: Nimbadon lavarackorum was a fossil marsupial that lived in Australia during the Miocene, between 18 and 15 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from limestone of the Carl Creek formation at Riversleigh. Adults weighed about 100 kilograms, and the animal ate plants and is thought to have climbed trees, making it a relative of the koala.
kelenken: Kelenken guillermoi was a flightless terror bird that lived during the Miocene, roughly 15 to 14 million years ago. Its fossils come from sandstone of the Collon Cura Formation in Patagonia and the Pampas. Adults reached about 250 kilograms, and its skull measured 71 centimeters, making it the largest known of its kind.
eohippus: Roughly 53 to 50 million years ago, this small four-toed dawn horse roamed the forests of western North America. Its fossils have turned up in the mudstone of the Willwood Formation in the Bighorn Basin. Adults weighed about 8 kilograms, and they fed on herbs.
hyaenodon_gigas: Lived during the Oligocene, roughly 33 to 30 million years ago, and left its remains in conglomerate rock of the Hsanda Gol Formation on the Mongolian steppe. As a carnivore weighing about 600 kilograms, it was the largest hyaenodont known, and its heavy build and powerful jaws suggest it crushed bone as it fed.
diceratherium: Diceratherium annectens was a plant-eating rhinoceros-like fossil taxon that lived during the Oligocene, roughly 28 to 20 million years ago. Adults reached about 800 kg, and the species carried a pair of nasal horns. Its remains have been recovered from volcanic ash deposits within the John Day Formation of the Pacific Northwest.
entelodon: Known from fossils, the Entelodon magnus lived across Europe during the Eocene, roughly 35 to 30 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone in the Phosphorites du Quercy formation. Adults could reach about 500 kg, and its omnivorous diet and likely scavenging habits, along with the bony knobs on its cheeks, earned it the nickname "hell pig."
adcrocuta: Known only from fossils, this extinct hyena lived in Europe during the Miocene, roughly 9 to 7 million years ago. Its remains have turned up in the mudstone of the Pikermi Formation. Adults weighed about 80 kilograms, and the animal is thought to have lived in packs and cracked bones to get at marrow, feeding largely on scavenged carcasses.
elasmotherium: Elasmotherium sibiricum was a grazing herbivore that roamed the steppe, with a body mass of about 4500 kilograms as an adult. Its most striking feature was a single enormous horn on its forehead, which earned it the nickname the Siberian unicorn. Fossils of this animal have been recovered from conglomerate deposits of the Pavlodar Pleistocene terraces in the Kazakh steppe.
heliobatis: Heliobatis lived during the Eocene, roughly 53 to 48 million years ago, and is known only from fossils. Its remains were preserved in shale of the Green River Formation in western North America. This freshwater stingray swam through ancient lake waters, fed on other animals, and grew to about 1 kilogram as an adult.
hippopotamus_gorgops: The extinct hippo Hippopotamus gorgops lived during the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 0.8 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone in the Bed I and Bed II layers of Olduvai Gorge on the East African savanna. This herbivore weighed about 4500 kilograms as an adult, and it is known to have been a swimmer with eyes set high on its head.
pakicetus: Pakicetus attocki lived roughly 50 to 49 million years ago during the Eocene, and its fossils turn up in marine sediments of the Kuldana Formation on the Indian subcontinent. This carnivore weighed about 50 kilograms and was roughly the size of a wolf. Its remains help show how early whales evolved from land-dwelling mammals that could both walk and swim.
propalaeotherium: Propalaeotherium lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 48 to 47 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from shale of the Messel Pit Formation, where preserved stomach contents reveal a diet of plants. Adults weighed about 30 kilograms, and this early relative of the horse likely roamed forested country.
quinkana: Quinkana fortirostrata was an extinct land-dwelling crocodile that roamed Australia during the Pleistocene, between 2 and 0.04 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Darling Downs deposits, known as the Chinchilla Sand formation. Adults reached about 3 metres in length and weighed roughly 300 kilograms, and it fed on meat.
titanophoneus: Titanophoneus potens was a predatory dinocephalian that lived during the Permian, roughly 265 to 260 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Isheevo Formation in Europe. An adult could reach about 400 kilograms, and it fed on other animals.
andrewsarchus: Known from fossil skulls found in the mudstones of the Irdin Manha Formation on the Mongolian steppe, this extinct creature lived between 45 and 40 million years ago during the Eocene. Its diet is thought to have been omnivorous. Based only on skull measurements, researchers estimate it may have weighed around 600 kilograms, making it the largest land predator of its mesonychian-like group.
baltic_gecko: The Baltic amber gecko lived during the Eocene, somewhere between 44 and 38 million years ago. Its remains come to us from the Baltic amber formation in Europe, where it was trapped and preserved inside hardened tree resin. Adults weighed about 0.003 kilograms, and the species is thought to have hunted insects while living in the trees.
titanoides: Titanoides was a saber-tusked pantodont that lived in western North America during the Paleocene, roughly 58 to 56 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Fort Union Formation. An herbivore, it weighed about 200 kilograms as an adult.
barytherium: Known only from fossils, Barytherium grave lived during the Eocene, roughly 37 to 34 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from sandstone of the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region, near the Nile valley. This herbivore weighed about 2000 kg as an adult and is thought to have swum, while its four tusks set it apart.
dominican_anole: Preserved in amber from the La Toca Formation of the Caribbean, this fossil lizard lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 15 million years ago. It was an arboreal creature that climbed through trees, and it fed on insects. Adults weighed only about 5 grams, so they were tiny even among their relatives.
crocodylus_thorbjarnarsoni: Thorbjarnarson's crocodile lived during the Pliocene, roughly 4 to 1.8 million years ago, and its remains have been recovered from sandstone in the Bed I and Bed II formations at Olduvai Gorge on the East African savanna. This carnivore grew to an estimated adult mass of 1500 kg and a length of 7.5 m. It was a swimmer, and it is recorded as having preyed on hominins.
notharctus: Notharctus tenebrosus was a lemur-like adapid that lived in the trees during the Eocene, roughly 50 to 45 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the mudstones of the Bridger Formation in western North America. Adults weighed about 3 kilograms, and the animal is thought to have fed mainly on fruit.
waimanu: Waimanu manneringi lived in the seas off what is now New Zealand between 62 and 58 million years ago, during the Paleocene. Its fossils come from marine sediments of the Waipara Greensand formation. This early penguin weighed about 10 kilograms as an adult, fed on fish, and swam through the water, making it one of the earliest known penguins.
anteosaurus: Living roughly 265 to 260 million years ago, this Permian predator was a five-meter dinocephalian that weighed around 500 kilograms as an adult. Its fossils turn up in mudstone of the Abrahamskraal Formation within the Karoo Supergroup of Southern Africa. It was a carnivore, hunting other animals in the ancient landscapes of what is now that region.
gorgonops: Gorgonops torvus lived in Southern Africa during the Permian, roughly 258 to 254 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Teekloof Formation within the Karoo Supergroup. This carnivore weighed about 55 kg as an adult and was equipped with long saber teeth, marking it as a gorgonopsian.
ambulocetus: Roughly 48 to 47 million years ago, Ambulocetus natans prowled the coastal waters that once covered the Indian subcontinent. Its fossils turn up in marine sediments of the Kuldana Formation, a clue that this carnivore spent much of its life near the sea. Adults could reach about 300 kilograms, and the animal was able to both swim and walk, earning it the nickname walking whale.
coelodonta: Long before the last ice age ended, this herbivore roamed the cold grasslands of Eurasia. Its remains turn up in the Yedoma deposits of Yakutia, where permafrost has preserved them in Siberian taiga country. Adults weighed about 2000 kilograms, and a thick coat and two horns helped it survive on the tundra and steppe.
palaeomastodon: Palaeomastodon beadnelli lived during the Eocene, roughly 35 to 30 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region, near the Nile valley. This herbivore weighed about 2000 kilograms as an adult and carried a short trunk along with tusks. Its remains show it was an early member of the elephant lineage.
coryphodon: Coryphodon lived in the Eocene, roughly 56 to 50 million years ago, and its remains have turned up in the mudstone of the Willwood Formation in the Bighorn Basin of western North America.
