This plant eater grew to around 500 kilograms as an adult. Its tusks and its habit of swimming suggest it spent much of its time in swampy wetlands.
diplomystus: Known only from fossils, this herring relative lived during the Eocene, roughly 53 to 48 million years ago. Its remains are preserved in shale of the Green River Formation in western North America. Adults weighed about half a kilogram, and it swam through the water hunting other animals.
gomphotherium_angustidens: A fossil proboscidean from the Miocene, living roughly 16 to 13 million years ago, Gomphotherium angustidens is known from remains found in the sandstone of the Sansan Formation in Europe. Adults reached about 4000 kilograms and fed on herbs. This relative of elephants had four tusks and is thought to have lived in herds.
doedicurus: Doedicurus, a heavily armoured herbivore, roamed the grasslands of what is now Patagonia and the Pampas during the Pleistocene. Its fossils have turned up in the mudstone of the Lujan Formation. Adults weighed about 1400 kilograms, and a spiked club at the end of its tail served as a formidable defence.
moeritherium: Moeritherium lyonsi was a tapir-sized proboscidean that lived during the Eocene, roughly 37 to 34 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region near the Nile valley. Adults weighed about 235 kg, and the animal is thought to have fed on herbs and to have been capable of swimming.
cotylorhynchus: Cotylorhynchus romeri was a huge, barrel-bodied caseid that lived during the Permian, roughly 280 to 275 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Hennessey Formation in the southern United States. Adults could reach about 600 kilograms, and the animal is thought to have been a herbivore that moved in herds.
merycoidodon: Merycoidodon culbertsoni lived during the Eocene, roughly 34 to 30 million years ago, and its fossils turn up in mudstone of the White River Group across the Great Plains. This herbivore weighed about 80 kg as an adult and is thought to have moved in herds. Its sheep-like build earned it a place among the oreodonts.
pristinailurus: Known only from fossils, Pristinailurus bristoli lived during the Miocene, roughly 7 to 4.5 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from mudstone at the Gray Fossil Site in eastern North America. Weighing about 5 kg as an adult, this omnivore spent much of its life in trees and is considered the earliest known relative of the red panda.
paleoparadoxia: Paleoparadoxia was a heavy, herbivorous fossil mammal that lived roughly 16 to 15 million years ago during the Miocene. Its remains have been recovered from the Round Mountain Silt, part of the Sharktooth Hill Bonebed in western North America, where they were buried in marine sediment. Adults weighed about 1000 kilograms, and the animal is known to have been a swimmer and a member of the desmostylians.
moropus: Long extinct, Moropus lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 18 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Harrison Formation on the Great Plains. An herbivore that weighed about 800 kg, it was a clawed odd-toed browser that fed on plants.
indohyus: An ancient mammal known from fossils, Indohyus lived roughly 48 to 47 million years ago during the Eocene. Its remains were recovered from the Kuldana Formation on the Indian subcontinent, in marine sediment. It ate plants, weighed about 10 kilograms as an adult, and is a close relative of the raoellids, the group that gave rise to modern whales.
brontops: Brontops robustus was a large, herbivorous brontothere that lived roughly 38 to 34 million years ago during the Eocene. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the White River Group, including the Chadron and Brule Formations, across the Great Plains. Adults reached about 2500 kilograms, and the animals are thought to have moved in herds.
phorusrhacos: Phorusrhacos longissimus was a flightless bird of the Miocene, living roughly 17 to 15 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Santa Cruz Formation in Patagonia and the Pampas. Standing about 2.4 meters tall and weighing around 130 kilograms, this carnivore earned the name terror bird.
basilosaurus_isis: Long before whales swam the modern seas, Basilosaurus isis cruised the warm waters that once covered northern Africa. Its fossils come from mudstone of the Birket Qarun Formation in the Nile valley, dating to between 38 and 34 million years ago. This carnivore stretched about 17 metres long and weighed roughly 5800 kilograms, with a serpentine body and tiny hindlimbs.
borealosuchus: A fossil crocodylian from the Eocene, Borealosuchus wilsoni lived roughly 53 to 48 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from shale of the Green River Formation in western North America. This carnivore grew to about 2.5 meters long and weighed around 100 kilograms as an adult, and it was a capable swimmer.
equus_simplicidens: The Hagerman horse lived during the Pliocene, roughly 3.7 to 3 million years ago, and it is known from fossils recovered in mudstone of the Glenns Ferry Formation at the Hagerman Horse Quarry in western North America. It grazed on plants and grew to about 400 kilograms as an adult. Its build was zebra-like, and it likely moved in herds.
archaeotherium: Archaeotherium mortoni lived during the Eocene, roughly 37 to 28 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from mudstone in the White River Group, including the Chadron and Brule Formations of the Great Plains. This entelodont was an omnivore that could reach about 400 kilograms. Some of the fossils preserve bite scars, offering a glimpse of the rough encounters these animals had.
dominican_butterfly: Preserved in Dominican amber, this extinct insect was found in the La Toca Formation of the Caribbean. It lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 15 million years ago, and fed on nectar as an adult. Weighing only about a tenth of a milligram, it was a tiny flying creature whose delicate wings were sealed in tree resin long ago.
andalgalornis: A fossil species from the Miocene, roughly 6 to 5 million years ago, Andalgalornis steulleti was a flightless terror bird. Its remains have been recovered from sandstone of the Andalhuala Formation, across the Pampas and Gran Chaco. It was a carnivore weighing about 40 kg as an adult, and it was known for its speed.
sivatherium: The Sivatherium was a extinct giraffid that lived across the Indian subcontinent during the Pliocene, roughly 3 to 0.5 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Siwalik Group, within the Nagri and Dhok Pathan Formations. Weighing about 1250 kg as an adult, it was the heaviest of all giraffids, and its moose-like horns set it apart from its relatives. It fed on herbs.
thylacosmilus: Thylacosmilus atrox was a marsupial saber-tooth that lived during the Pliocene, roughly 5 to 3 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the mudstone of the Chapadmalal Formation in Patagonia and the Pampas. An adult weighed about 100 kilograms, and it was a carnivore thought to have hunted by ambush.
argentavis: Argentavis magnificens lived during the Miocene, roughly 6 to 5 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Andalhuala Formation in the Pampas and Gran Chaco. Adults weighed about 70 kg and it is thought to have fed mainly by scavenging. With a wingspan of 6 to 7 metres, it is the largest flying bird known.
palaeeudyptes_klekowskii: Living roughly 40 to 37 million years ago during the Eocene, this giant penguin stood about 1.4 meters tall and weighed around 80 kilograms. Its fossils come from sandstone of the La Meseta Formation in Antarctica. It fed on fish and was a strong swimmer.
edaphosaurus: Edaphosaurus pogonias lived during the Carboniferous period, roughly 300 to 275 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. An adult could weigh around 200 kilograms, and a large sail of spines rose from its back, with crossbar spines running across it. This plant eater is known from that striking sail alone.
meganeura: A giant insect from the Carboniferous, Meganeura monyi lived roughly 305 to 300 million years ago. Its fossils come from shale of the Commentry Formation in the Commentry Basin of Europe. It was a carnivore that weighed about 0.15 kg and spread wings to a span of around 65 cm, earning it the name giant griffinfly.
dinocrocuta: Dinocrocuta, a giant hyena-like predator of the Miocene, lived roughly 13 to 7 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Liushu Formation in the Linxia Basin, within the Himalaya and Tibet region. Adults weighed around 140 kg, and the animal is thought to have fed largely on carrion.
sphenacodon: Sphenacodon ferox lived roughly 300 to 295 million years ago, during the Carboniferous period. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Cutler Formation in the southern United States. This meat eater reached an adult mass of about 80 kilograms and carried a prominent sail along its back.
josephoartigasia: Josephoartigasia monesi was a fossil rodent that lived during the Pliocene, roughly 4 to 2 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from mudstone of the San Jose Formation in the Southern Cone. It is the largest rodent known, with an adult mass of about 1000 kg, and it ate plants and is thought to have been able to swim.
scutosaurus: Scutosaurus karpinskii was a heavy, armoured pareiasaur that lived during the Permian, roughly 255 to 252 million years ago. Adults could reach about 600 kg, and the animal bore spikes along its body. Its fossils come from mudstone of the Salarevo Formation in Europe, and it is thought to have been a plant eater that moved in herds.
dimetrodon_limbatus: Dimetrodon limbatus lived during the Permian period, roughly 285 to 275 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. This carnivore could reach an adult mass of about 250 kilograms, making it a top predator of its time. Its tall sail marks it as a distinctive animal, and despite its lizard-like look it was not a dinosaur.
dromornis: A towering flightless bird from the Miocene, Dromornis stirtoni once roamed the lands now preserved as the Alcoota Local Fauna in Australia. Its fossils were found in limestone of the Waite Formation, dating from 8 to 7 million years ago. This herbivore stood about 3 meters tall and weighed roughly 600 kilograms, earning it a reputation as the largest bird known.
amphicyon_giganteus: Amphicyon giganteus was a fossil species that lived during the Miocene, roughly 16 to 13 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from sandstone of the Sansan Formation in Europe. Known as a bear dog, this carnivore is estimated to have weighed about 200 kg as an adult.
barawertornis: Barawertornis was a large, flightless bird from the Oligocene, living roughly 25 to 23 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Etadunna Formation in Australia. Adults weighed about 70 kilograms, and the species fed on plants.
dominican_scorpion: Preserved whole inside Dominican amber, this scorpion lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 15 million years ago. Its remains come from the La Toca Formation in the Caribbean, where resin trapped it and kept its body intact. Adults weighed about 2 grams, and the species was carnivorous and venomous.
anoplotherium: Anoplotherium lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 38 to 35 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from the Gypse de Montmartre formation, where they are preserved within limestone. Weighing about 80 kg as an adult, this herbivore fed on plants and likely moved through forest habitats, with a heavy, two-toed tail.
diictodon: Diictodon was a small, tusked dicynodont that lived in what is now southern Africa during the Permian, roughly 257 to 253 million years ago. Its fossils come from mudstone of the Teekloof Formation in the Karoo Supergroup. Adults weighed about 1 kg, and the animal likely fed on plants and lived in burrows, possibly in social groups.
carbonemys: Carbonemys cofrinii lived during the Paleocene, roughly 60 to 58 million years ago, and its remains were found in coal of the Cerrejon Formation in the Caribbean. This side-necked turtle measured about 1.7 meters long and weighed around 1000 kilograms as an adult. It was an omnivore that swam through its waters, protected by a shell, and it is thought to have eaten crocodiles.
acinonyx_pardinensis: The giant cheetah lived in Europe during the Pliocene, roughly three to one and a half million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone deposits of the Upper Valdarno Basin. Adults weighed around 120 kilograms, and the animal was a carnivore built for running long distances across open ground.
meganeuropsis: Meganeuropsis permiana lived during the Permian period, roughly 283 to 280 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from shale of the Wellington Formation near Elmo in the Great Plains. This carnivorous flyer weighed about 0.04 kg as an adult and held the record as the largest known insect, with a wingspan of 71 cm.
mesohippus: Living roughly 37 to 32 million years ago during the Eocene, this three-toed early horse left its fossils in mudstone of the White River Group, in the Chadron and Brule Formations across the Great Plains. It grazed on herbs and weighed about 50 kilograms as an adult. Mesohippus shows the gradual path that led toward modern horses, with its three toes marking a stage between the older, more numerous-toed forms and today's single-hoofed animals.
dinictis: An extinct predator from the Eocene, Dinictis felina lived roughly 34 to 30 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone within the White River Group, in the Chadron and Brule Formations of the Great Plains. Weighing around 20 kilograms as an adult, this meat-eater was a nimravid, often called a false saber-tooth cat.
platybelodon: Platybelodon lived roughly 13 to 11 million years ago during the Miocene. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Tung Gur Formation on the Mongolian steppe. This herbivore weighed about 3500 kilograms as an adult and had flattened, shovel-shaped tusks, which it likely used to scoop up plants from swampy ground in herds.
gigantopithecus: The largest primate known to science, Gigantopithecus blacki roamed the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 0.3 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from limestone deposits in the Liucheng Gigantopithecus Cave formation in the lowlands of China. Adults may have weighed around 300 kilograms, and the animal is thought to have lived on the ground and fed on plants, possibly bamboo. Although it was an ape, it was not a hominin, meaning it sat outside the human lineage.
lycaenops: Lycaenops ornatus lived in the Permian, roughly 260 to 256 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Teekloof Formation in Southern Africa. This carnivore weighed about 25 kilograms as an adult and hunted with long, saber-like teeth. It is known as a fast member of the gorgonopsians.
embolotherium: Embolotherium andrewsi lived during the Eocene, roughly 37 to 34 million years ago, and its remains have been recovered from mudstone in the Ulan Gochu Formation of the Mongolian steppe. This herbivore weighed around 3500 kilograms as an adult. It belonged to the brontotheres and carried a distinctive bony ram-like horn on its nose.
stupendemys: Stupendemys geographicus lived during the Miocene, between 13 and 7 million years ago, and its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Solimões Formation in the Amazon basin. This plant-eating turtle could reach about 1145 kilograms as an adult and measured roughly 3.3 meters across, with a shell that was built for life in the water. Its side-necked form and the horns found on males make it one of the more unusual freshwater turtles known from the fossil record.
pachycrocuta: Pachycrocuta brevirostris was a fossil hyena that lived during the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 0.4 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone deposits at Zhoukoudian Locality 1 in the China lowlands. Weighing about 190 kg as an adult, it was the largest hyena known, and it is recognized as a powerful bone crusher that fed mainly by scavenging.
baltic_termite: Preserved in Baltic amber, this fossil termite lived during the Eocene, roughly 44 to 38 million years ago. Its remains were found in the amber deposits of Europe, where it was trapped and sealed in resin. It fed on herbs and weighed about one gram as an adult.
diadectes: Known only from fossils, Diadectes phaseolinus lived during the Permian, roughly 290 to 280 million years ago. Its remains come from mudstone in the Clear Fork Group of the southern United States. This early herbivorous tetrapod is thought to have weighed about 120 kg as an adult and likely walked on land while feeding on plants.
pelagornis_sandersi: Pelagornis sandersi lived during the Oligocene, roughly 25 to 24 million years ago, and its fossils turn up in the marine sediments of the Chandler Bridge Formation in eastern North America. This bony-toothed seabird fed on fish and weighed about 40 kilograms as an adult. It could fly with a wingspan of 6.4 meters, one of the largest known for any flying bird.
dimetrodon_milleri: Dimetrodon milleri lived during the Permian, roughly 285 to 280 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Clear Fork Group in the southern United States. This carnivore weighed about 25 kg as an adult and was known for the tall sail along its back.
baltic_lizard: The Baltic amber lizard is known only from fossils, and it lived during the Eocene, somewhere between 44 and 38 million years ago. Its remains have been found preserved inside Baltic amber in Europe. Adults weighed about 0.005 kg, and this small reptile fed on insects.
titanis: Titanis walleri was a flightless bird that stood about 2.5 meters tall and weighed roughly 150 kilograms as an adult. Its fossils come from the Santa Fe River sites near Gainesville, Florida, where they are preserved in mudstone from the Pliocene, between 5 and 1.8 million years ago. It was a carnivore and is considered North America's last large predatory bird.
proconsul: Proconsul heseloni lived roughly 18 to 17 million years ago during the Miocene. Its fossils come from sandstone of the Hiwegi Formation on Rusinga Island, in what is now East Africa. This tailless early ape spent its life in the trees, and adults weighed about 11 kg. Its diet was mainly fruit.
dominican_gecko: Preserved in amber from the La Toca Formation of the Caribbean, this tree-dwelling lizard lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 15 million years ago. Its diet was insects, and adults weighed only about 2 grams. The fossil record of this tiny gecko survives because it was trapped in tree resin that hardened into amber.
simbakubwa: Known only from fossils, this extinct predator lived in what is now East Africa roughly 23 to 22 million years ago during the Miocene. Its remains were recovered from sandstone of the Meswa Bridge formation. Weighing about 1500 kilograms as an adult, it was the largest hyaenodont ever identified and was a hypercarnivore that fed mainly on meat.
puijila: Puijila lived during the Oligocene, roughly 24 to 22 million years ago, and its remains come from limestone of the Haughton Formation in the Arctic. This fossil animal weighed about 40 kg as an adult and fed on fish. Its build suggests a swimmer that moved on land in an otter-like way, a useful clue to how early seals began their transition to the water.
uintatherium: Roaming western North America between 47 and 42 million years ago, this heavy herbivore weighed about 2000 kilograms as an adult. Its fossils turn up in the mudstone of the Bridger Formation. Three pairs of horns crowned its skull, and long saber-like canine teeth set it apart from its plant-eating relatives.
hyaenodon_horridus: Hyaenodon horridus was a carnivorous fossil mammal that roamed the Great Plains during the Eocene, between 36 and 30 million years ago. Its remains come from mudstone within the White River Group, in the Chadron and Brule Formations. Adults weighed about 50 kg, and their massive skulls mark them as a hyaenodont, a group of predators with powerful jaws.
carcharodon_hastalis: Known only from fossil teeth and fragments, the broad-toothed mako lived during the Miocene, roughly 20 to 3 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from marine sediments of the Pisco Formation in the Andes. It was a carnivore that could reach an adult mass of about 1500 kg, and it is considered an ancestor of the great white shark.
hoplophoneus: Hoplophoneus primaevus was a nimravid, a saber-toothed cat that lived in the Eocene, roughly 34 to 30 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the White River Group, including the Chadron and Brule Formations, across the Great Plains. Adults weighed about 30 kilograms, and the animal was a carnivore.
arsinoitherium: Long extinct, this heavy herbivore roamed the Eocene landscape about 36 to 30 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Jebel Qatrani Formation in the Fayum region, near the Nile valley. Adults weighed around 1500 kilograms, and the animal carried two enormous horns while feeding on plants in swampy habitats.
gigantopithecus_bilaspurensis: Known only from fossils, this ground-dwelling ape lived during the Miocene, roughly 9 to 6 million years ago. Its remains were recovered from sandstone of the Siwalik Group, in the Nagri and Dhok Pathan Formations of the Indian subcontinent. Adults reached about 200 kilograms, and the animal is thought to have fed on plants.
megalochelys: Megalochelys atlas was a giant tortoise that lived during the Pliocene, roughly 3 to 0.5 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from sandstone of the Siwalik Group, including the Nagri and Dhok Pathan Formations, on the Indian subcontinent. This herbivore grew to about 2000 kg and measured around 2.7 m in length, with a massive shell.
hassianycteris: Known only from fossils, this bat lived during the Eocene, roughly 48 to 47 million years ago. Its remains were preserved in shale of the Messel Pit Formation in Europe. Weighing about 0.04 kg as an adult, it hunted insects on the wing, flying fast in open air during the night.
knightia: Knightia lived in the Eocene, roughly 53 to 48 million years ago, and its fossils are preserved in the shale of the Green River Formation in western North America. This small herring-like fish swam in enormous schools and feeds on fine particles. Adults weighed about 0.1 kg, and it is the most common fossil fish found in that formation.
moschops: Living about 265 to 260 million years ago in the Permian, this heavy herbivore left its remains in the mudstones of the Abrahamskraal Formation in Southern Africa. Adults could reach roughly 400 kilograms, carried on a barrel-shaped body. Its thick skull and suspected herd living make it a striking early relative of the mammal line.
phoberomys: Living roughly 8 to 6 million years ago during the Miocene, this fossil rodent weighed about 700 kilograms as an adult. Its remains come from mudstone of the Urumaco Formation in the Caribbean region. It ate plants and is thought to have swum, making it a giant relative of the paca.
eurohippus: Eurohippus messelensis lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 48 to 47 million years ago. Its remains come from shale of the Messel Pit Formation, where a fossil has preserved an unborn foal inside the mother. Adults weighed about 8 kilograms, and this herbivore fed on plants in forest habitats.
palaeotherium: Lived in Europe during the Eocene, roughly 38 to 35 million years ago, and is known only from fossils. Its remains were recovered from the limestone of the Gypse de Montmartre formation. This odd-toed herbivore weighed about 400 kg as an adult, and it was a forest dweller that fed on plants.
deinotherium_bozasi: Roughly ten tonnes at adulthood, this herbivore roamed the East African savanna during the Pliocene, between about 3.8 and 1 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from the Laetolil Beds, where they were preserved in volcanic ash. It was the last of the deinotheres, a long-lived lineage of elephant relatives.
janjucetus: Janjucetus hunderi lived in the seas during the Oligocene, roughly 27 to 25 million years ago. Its fossils come from marine sediments of the Jan Juc Formation in Australia. An adult weighed about 500 kg, and it hunted other animals as a carnivore. It was a swimming, toothed relative of the baleen whales.
smilodon_populator: Smilodon populator lived across the Pleistocene, roughly between 1 and 0.013 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Lujan Formation in Patagonia and the Pampas. As a carnivore weighing about 400 kg, it was the largest of the saber-toothed cats, and it likely hunted by ambushing its prey.
baltic_ant: Preserved in Baltic amber from Europe, this extinct ant lived during the Eocene, roughly 44 to 38 million years ago. Its fossils show a creature that weighed about half a milligram as an adult. Its diet is classed as omnivorous, and the notes record that these ants appear in amber alongside flies and swarm behavior.
tiarajudens: Tiarajudens eccentricus lived during the Permian, roughly 265 to 260 million years ago, and it is known from fossils preserved in mudstone of the Rio do Rasto Formation in South America. This plant eater weighed about 50 kilograms as an adult. Despite its long, saber-like teeth, it was an herbivore, a surprising combination that sets it apart from the meat-eating saber-toothed animals most people picture.
palorchestes: Known only from fossils, this browsing animal lived across the Pleistocene, roughly 2 to 0.04 million years ago. Its remains have been recovered from limestone deposits at the Naracoorte Caves in Australia, including the Wet Cave and Victoria Fossil Cave. It was an herbivore that grew to about 600 kg, and it had claws and a trunk-like snout suited to feeding on plants.
rodhocetus: Rodhocetus kasrani was a semi-aquatic protocetid that lived during the Eocene, roughly 47 to 46 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from limestone of the Habib Rahi Formation on the Indian subcontinent. This carnivore weighed about 600 kilograms as an adult and is known for its swimming habits.
estemmenosuchus: Estemmenosuchus lived in what is now Europe during the Permian, roughly 265 to 260 million years ago. Its fossils have been recovered from mudstone of the Isheevo Formation. This horned dinocephalian is thought to have eaten plants and grew to an adult mass of about 600 kilograms.
